newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli cabinet approves Hebron deal with PLO.
newsitem.headline: Israeli cabinet approves Hebron deal with PLO.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu crushed a fierce right-wing revolt to win cabinet approval for a Hebron withdrawal pact with the Palestinians.
Ministers accepted the agreement to carry out the long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town by a vote of 11-7 on Thursday after a stormy meeting lasting 12 hours.
Science Minister Binyamin Begin, son of the late prime minister Menachem Begin, resigned, a cabinet official said.
Begin led the onslaught against Netanyahu for sealing the U.S.-brokered Hebron deal with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Wednesday. Arafat's cabinet approved the accord in Gaza.
Netanyahu cancelled a post-cabinet news conference as it became clear the acrimonious meeting which started at lunchtime on Wednesday would overrun into Thursday.
The wrangling reflected the deep split in Netanyahu's Likud-led coalition over ceding land to Palestinians that many Israelis believe to be theirs by biblical right.
The agreement was expected to win backing in Israel's parliament later on Thursday thanks to support from the Labour opposition which initiated peace moves with the Palestinians.

Knesset approval will be a green light for the Israeli army to begin its long-delayed redeployment from four-fifths of Hebron. The deal also lays down a timetable for Israel to hand over rural areas of the West Bank to Palestinians in three stages over the next 18 months.

This constitutes an ideological U-turn for Netanyahu, who had always opposed the land-for-peace formula with Arafat, a man he used to brand a terrorist. The United States and many Western and Arab governments hailed the accord as a sign that Middle East peacemaking was back on track.

In Hebron, residents said the army was preparing to leave. Extra soldiers were on the streets to prevent protests by Jewish settlers who have vowed to stay on in the heart of the city of 100,000 Palestinians.
"It's a sad day when a Jewish government takes this very grave decision," settler Moshe Ben-Zimra said.

"Netanyahu will be remembered as the first prime minister who abandoned the legacy of the fathers to outsiders, who abandoned Jewish lives in the Land of Israel," he told Israel Radio. About 400 militant settlers live in the centre of Hebron, site of the biblical patriarchs, who are revered by Jews and Moslems.
Palestinians put up posters of Arafat, who is expected to visit the city within a week of withdrawal.
Israeli security sources said a pullback to the 20 percent of Hebron which includes the holy places and Jewish enclaves would be swift.

Cabinet secretary Danny Naveh said Israel would soon begin to discuss the principles of so-called "final status" talks to seek a permanent solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. He said Israel hoped to conclude this before the second phase of the further withdrawals.
But Palestinians expect further wrangling over the extent of those withdrawals, which Israel insists that it alone will determine.
Chief Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said after the cabinet vote that Palestinians would be watching how Israel carried out the deal which still had many outstanding issues.
"It's essential to see now deeds rather than words," he told Reuters.
